terms.gloss: be master, rule; of things, prevail, take over
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent; in + abl. or inter + acc.
evidence: Verg. G. 1.154: sterilēs dominantur avēnae (Lewis & Short)
Vulg. Prov. 16.32: quī dominātur animō suō
terms.comment: From dominus: to be lord and master. Of things it means to prevail, to take over a place, as weeds a field or a passion the mind. Of people it often has the overtone of tyranny, as dominātiō does (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: reign; figuratively, have the mastery, predominate
evidence: Cic. Or. 128: in quō ūnō rēgnat ōrātiō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In this sense the thing that dominates is the subject: rēgnat ōrātiō, the speech holds sway.

terms.gloss: have the most power or influence; be the dominant one
terms.grammar: verb phrase: possum, posse, potuī; apud + acc.
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 4: quī apud mē … plūrimum possunt (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: inter nitentia culta īnfēlīx lolium et sterilēs dominantur avēnae
phrases.english: among the gleaming crops the wretched darnel and barren wild oats take over

phrases.latin: Melior est patiēns virō fortī, et quī dominātur animō suō expugnātōre urbium.
phrases.english: Better is the patient man than the strong, and he who rules his own spirit than one who takes cities.

sources: Lewis & Short: dominor · Lewis & Short: regno · Lewis & Short: possum
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-vulgata), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
